The linked engine articles explain component layout and filter diagnosis. They are not a complete base-engine oil drain-and-refill walkthrough; use the oil-change instructions and specifications for the fitted engine.
guides.title: Engine oil and filter: make the oil-life monitor useful
guides.summary: Plan an oil change around actual use, choose the correct oil and filter, and reset the monitor only after the work is done.
guides.introduction: Oil is doing several jobs while the engine runs: keeping moving surfaces apart, carrying heat away and transporting contamination to the filter. The useful habit is to treat the oil and filter as a service pair, then keep an eye on the level between changes. The oil-life display estimates when that pair needs service; it does not tell you how much oil is in the sump.
guides.why: Short trips, idling, temperature and engine load affect how quickly oil is used up. That is why a fixed mileage picked from a friend’s driving pattern can be the wrong plan for your car.

when.summary: Follow the oil-life message. The maximum is one year or 10,000 mi (16,000 km) between services.
notes: After a service message, arrange the change within two weeks or 500 mi (800 km).
If the monitor is inoperative or was reset prematurely, use six months or 5,000 mi (8,000 km) from the last actual change.
The mileage ranges in the schedule are estimates, not permission to ignore an earlier message.

prepare.title: Identify the engine
prepare.detail: Choose the oil grade, Ford specification, quantity and filter for the actual engine. Do not borrow the 5.2L oil procedure for a base-engine car.

prepare.title: Plan the complete job
prepare.detail: Arrange safe access, oil collection and disposal, the correct replacement filter, and the correct service instructions before draining anything.

steps.title: Confirm what is due
steps.body: Check the service record, odometer, date and oil-life message. Include the inspections that are due at an oil-change service.

steps.title: Change both service items
steps.body: Use the correct engine-specific oil-change instructions. A replacement filter and fresh oil work together; changing one is not a substitute for changing the other.

steps.title: Finish with verification and a record
steps.body: Confirm the final oil level and check the serviced area for leakage. Record the date, mileage and oil specification.

steps.title: Reset the display after the change
steps.body: With the vehicle safely parked, use the information display’s Settings → Vehicle → Oil Life Reset entry and hold OK to reset. Menu presentation can vary with equipment.

watchFor.title: A level that keeps changing
watchFor.body: Repeated topping up or an unexpectedly rising level deserves investigation; an oil-life reset cannot correct it.

watchFor.title: An oil-pressure warning
watchFor.body: Treat a pressure warning as a problem requiring immediate action, not as a reminder that an oil change is nearly due.

Identify the 5.0L engine components.

notes: Never remove the dipstick or filler cap while the engine is running. Overfilling can damage the engine.
guides.title: Check engine oil level between services
guides.summary: A simple level check answers a different question from the oil-life display: is there enough oil in the engine?
guides.introduction: An oil change establishes a fresh starting point, but the engine still needs the right quantity of oil afterward. Checking the level lets you notice a developing change instead of discovering it when a warning appears. Make the check under consistent conditions so the readings are worth comparing.
guides.why: The dipstick measures oil quantity in the sump. The oil-life monitor estimates service timing. Neither reading replaces the other, and neither by itself diagnoses why a level is changing.

when.summary: Check monthly and before investigating a suspected oil-level problem.
notes: Continue the oil-and-filter service schedule separately.

prepare.title: Use a level location
prepare.detail: Park on level ground, set the parking brake and put the transmission in Park or Neutral. Bring the engine to normal operating temperature, switch it off and wait 15 minutes for oil to settle.

prepare.title: Have the correct oil available
prepare.detail: If topping up is necessary, confirm the engine’s required grade and specification first.

steps.title: Read the dipstick
steps.body: With the engine off, remove the dipstick, wipe it with a clean lint-free cloth, fully reinsert it, then remove it again to read the marked range.

steps.title: Decide whether oil is needed
steps.body: Between MIN and MAX is acceptable; do not add oil. At MIN, add the correct oil immediately.

steps.title: Top up cleanly if required
steps.body: Clean around the filler cap before opening it. Add the specified oil, recheck the level and avoid exceeding MAX.

steps.title: Close and record
steps.body: Fully seat the dipstick, secure the filler cap and clean up spillage. Record unusual additions so a changing level can be investigated.

watchFor.title: Repeated loss or a rising reading
watchFor.body: Either deserves investigation. Do not explain it away by resetting the oil-life display.

watchFor.title: Oil outside the engine
watchFor.body: Fresh wetness around a seal, filter or pan needs its source identified before a part is blamed.

Locate components on the 2.3L.
Locate components on the 5.0L.

notes: Only lubricate components equipped with the specified grease fittings. Dry stabilizer-bar bushings must not be treated as grease points.
If a temporary tire-mobility kit is fitted, check the sealant canister’s Use By date and replace expired sealant.
guides.title: Build a useful oil-service inspection
guides.summary: Use an oil change as a convenient checkpoint for the rest of the car, with observations that lead to decisions.
guides.introduction: The most valuable inspection produces a short, specific record: which part was checked, what was found and whether anything needs attention. “Looks fine” is less useful than recording tire wear, a dry or wet joint, or a hose that needs a closer look. Ford recommends a multi-point inspection alongside each scheduled service.
guides.why: Wear and small leaks develop between major replacement intervals. Looking at the car as a system helps avoid replacing one noisy part while missing the loose mounting or damaged boot nearby.

when.summary: At every oil-change service; a multi-point inspection is recommended.
notes: For this schedule, the oil-service interval must not exceed one year or 10,000 mi (16,000 km).

prepare.title: Bring the history
prepare.detail: Record current concerns, mileage, previous repairs and fluid additions.

prepare.title: Separate owner checks from workshop access
prepare.detail: Lights and washer operation are easy to review from outside the car. Underbody inspections need safe access and suitable support.

steps.title: Begin with things you can observe
steps.body: Check tire condition, exterior lamps, hazards, horn, warning-system operation, washer spray and wiping. Inspect the windshield for chips, cracks or pitting.

steps.title: Review the engine bay
steps.body: Include the accessory belts, battery performance, engine air filter, and radiator, cooler, heater and air-conditioning hoses. Look for fluid leaks and check the brake, coolant-reservoir, automatic-transmission and washer levels using each system’s correct method; top up only when required.

steps.title: Review the underbody and running gear
steps.body: Include brakes, exhaust and heat shields, steering, suspension, driveshaft joints, halfshaft boots and wheel-related condition. Record suspension leaks or damage.

steps.title: Turn findings into a plan
steps.body: Record what is normal, what needs diagnosis and which scheduled items are approaching. A service checklist is not an instruction to replace every part on it.

watchFor.title: The same item noted repeatedly
watchFor.body: A recurring leak, tire-wear pattern or noise needs a diagnostic plan instead of another vague note.

watchFor.title: Work that does not match the car
watchFor.body: Confirm fitted equipment before approving a fluid service, brake package or grease-point instruction.

procedures.purpose: Identify the rear suspension components that an inspection covers.
Follow suspension diagnosis when an inspection finds a concern.
Investigate brake-system findings.

notes: A tire-pressure warning system does not replace physical checks. Never work beneath a car supported only by a jack.
guides.title: Tires: pressure, tread and the right rotation
guides.summary: Check the tire’s condition and pressure first, then rotate only in a pattern allowed by its size and construction.
guides.introduction: Tires are the car’s contact with the road, so small changes here can make the whole car feel different. Pressure supports the load; tread and casing condition affect how the tire works. Rotation can help manage wear, but a Mustang’s front and rear wheel sizes may differ, and directional tires add another constraint.
guides.why: An uneven wear pattern can reveal an inflation, alignment or suspension concern. Rotating the tires without addressing the cause merely moves the evidence to another corner.

when.summary: Check pressure and wear monthly. At every oil service, inspect wear, measure tread depth and rotate where the fitted tire arrangement permits.
notes: Include the spare if fitted.

prepare.title: Read the vehicle label
prepare.detail: Use the correct cold pressures and approved tire sizes for the car, rather than the maximum pressure molded into the tire.

prepare.title: Identify rotation limits
prepare.detail: Compare front and rear sizes and check directional markings before choosing a rotation pattern.

steps.title: Inspect all tires
steps.body: Look across the tread and around visible sidewalls. Compare the wear pattern between corners rather than checking just the easiest tire to reach.

steps.title: Measure and record
steps.body: Check cold pressure and tread depth. Consistent records make developing uneven wear easier to spot.

steps.title: Rotate and recheck appropriately
steps.body: Use the correct wheel/tire procedure and permitted pattern. Complete any pressure-monitoring steps required for the fitted system.

watchFor.title: One edge wears faster
watchFor.body: Have the cause assessed; pressure, alignment and worn components can produce different patterns.

watchFor.title: Damage or continuing pressure loss
watchFor.body: Have the tire evaluated rather than repeatedly adding air and assuming it is safe.

procedures.purpose: Follow wheel and tire service instructions.
Investigate tire or wheel concerns.
Understand the tire-pressure monitoring system.

notes: Hub designs and fastener requirements vary by equipment. No repacking or automatic bearing-replacement schedule is supplied here.
guides.title: Wheel and hub checks: investigate noise and looseness
guides.summary: Check the wheel-end assembly as a whole before deciding that a bearing is responsible.
guides.introduction: A hum, shake or dragging sensation may seem to come from the wheel, but the tire, hub, brake and mounting all occupy the same area. A useful inspection narrows the possibilities. It does not start with a universal bearing-replacement mileage or a guess based only on the sound.
guides.why: The hub supports the wheel while allowing it to turn. Play, damage or drag can affect that job, but nearby brake or tire faults can produce similar clues.

when.summary: Inspect wheel-related condition at each oil-change service; investigate a new noise, looseness or drag sooner.
notes: Predominantly dusty or sandy operation calls for these checks every 5,000 mi (8,000 km).

prepare.title: Describe the symptom
prepare.detail: Note whether it changes with speed, braking, load or road surface.

prepare.title: Arrange safe access
prepare.detail: Wheel-off and raised-vehicle checks require the appropriate lifting points and support.

steps.title: Start with tire and wheel condition
steps.body: Confirm tire pressure, visible damage and unusual wear before blaming the bearing.

steps.title: Inspect the assembly methodically
steps.body: Use the diagnosis procedure to distinguish bearing play or noise from brake drag, loose components and tire concerns.

steps.title: Repair the confirmed cause
steps.body: Choose the exact hub or brake procedure for the fitted package, then verify that the original symptom has been resolved.

watchFor.title: A noise described as “definitely the bearing”
watchFor.body: The description is a starting clue. Confirmation matters before ordering a hub.

watchFor.title: Movement or drag
watchFor.body: Have it assessed promptly rather than waiting for the next routine service.

procedures.purpose: Service the standard front wheel bearing and hub.
Service the rear wheel bearing and hub.
Follow the suspension inspection and diagnosis path.

notes: Keep oil and grease off friction surfaces. Never leave a removed caliper hanging from its flexible hose.
guides.title: Brake inspection: pads, discs and hoses
guides.summary: Measure wear, look for damage and keep the fitted brake package straight before selecting parts.
guides.introduction: Brakes use friction to turn motion into heat. Pads are expected to wear, but an inspection also needs to consider the disc surface, hose condition and how the system is behaving. A change in noise is useful information; it does not automatically identify which part should be replaced.
guides.why: Uneven pad wear, damaged hoses and disc problems require different repairs. Treating every brake concern as “needs pads” can leave the cause in place.

when.summary: Inspect pads, discs, hoses and parking-brake condition at each oil-change service.
notes: A change in stopping performance, a fluid leak or a brake warning needs attention before the next scheduled service.

prepare.title: Identify the front brake package
prepare.detail: Use the 2-, 4- or 6-piston procedure that matches the car. Do not mix limits or hardware instructions.

prepare.title: Plan safe access
prepare.detail: Let hot components cool and arrange the correct lifting/support equipment before wheel-off inspection.

steps.title: Record how the concern behaves
steps.body: Note noise, pull, pulsation or dragging and when it happens.

steps.title: Inspect and measure
steps.body: Check the pads, discs and hoses using the applicable inspection limits. Compare inner and outer wear where the procedure requires it.

steps.title: Choose the matching repair
steps.body: Replace or service only what the inspection calls for, then complete the verification steps in the selected brake procedure.

watchFor.title: Fluid leakage or reduced braking
watchFor.body: Stop treating the issue as routine wear and have the braking system assessed.

watchFor.title: Uneven wear
watchFor.body: Investigate how the caliper and pads are moving instead of replacing the worn friction material alone.

notes: Do not use an uncontrolled roll test or rely on the parking brake as the sole means of supporting a raised vehicle.
guides.title: Parking brake: holding and releasing both matter
guides.summary: Check for a reliable hold, a full release and changes in control feel before reaching for an adjustment.
guides.introduction: The parking brake has two jobs: keep the parked car from moving and release cleanly when you are ready to drive. A change in lever feel, poor holding or drag after release can point to a concern. Simply taking up more cable adjustment does not establish that the mechanism is healthy.
guides.why: Dragging brakes generate heat and wear. A system that releases well but cannot hold the vehicle also needs attention, so the inspection must consider both directions of operation.

when.summary: Check operation every six months and during oil-service brake inspections.

prepare.title: Choose controlled conditions
prepare.detail: Use a safe location for an owner operation check. Raised-wheel and cable inspections belong in the dedicated procedure.

prepare.title: Note the change
prepare.detail: Describe new travel, stiffness, poor holding or failure to release rather than just asking for the cable to be tightened.

steps.title: Check normal application and release
steps.body: Observe the control’s feel and whether the system releases normally.

steps.title: Investigate a fault
steps.body: Use the symptom chart to inspect for damage or a mechanical cause. A warning lamp also needs the correct diagnosis.

steps.title: Adjust only as instructed
steps.body: If adjustment is called for, use the procedure for the fitted brake arrangement and verify both holding and release afterward.

watchFor.title: Drag after release
watchFor.body: Do not assume that the brake has released just because the lever is down.

watchFor.title: A brake warning that stays on
watchFor.body: The cause can include incomplete release or another brake-system problem; confirm it.

procedures.purpose: Diagnose parking-brake operation.
Use the standard cable-adjustment procedure when needed.
Understand and service the control mechanism.

notes: A scheduled coolant change is not a timed replacement instruction for the pump, radiator, thermostat or fan.
guides.title: Cooling-system checks between coolant changes
guides.summary: Check coolant level, strength and hose condition without turning every inspection into a pump or radiator replacement.
guides.introduction: The cooling system is a connected loop: coolant carries heat from the engine to the radiator, while the pump, thermostat, hoses and airflow all contribute. Looking at the loop as a whole is more useful than assuming a warm-running engine needs a particular part. Routine checks can reveal leakage or deterioration before the next scheduled coolant change.
guides.why: A low level, damaged hose or incorrect coolant concentration can limit cooling even when the pump is still turning. Repeated topping up hides the trend without explaining it.

when.summary: Inspect coolant strength and hoses at oil service. Check coolant level and strength every six months.
notes: Follow the coolant replacement schedule separately.

prepare.title: Let the system cool
prepare.detail: Do not open a hot cooling-system pressure cap.

prepare.title: Identify the correct fluid
prepare.detail: Confirm the coolant specification and concentration requirements for the engine before adding anything.

steps.title: Check the level consistently
steps.body: Use the specified cold-check conditions and the reservoir markings.

steps.title: Inspect the visible circuit
steps.body: Look for leakage or hose deterioration and have coolant strength checked with the appropriate method.

steps.title: Investigate a repeated problem
steps.body: If level keeps falling or temperature behavior changes, use cooling-system diagnosis to identify the cause before replacing parts.

watchFor.title: Repeated additions
watchFor.body: A system that keeps needing coolant deserves a leak investigation.

watchFor.title: Overheating or visible leakage
watchFor.body: Act on the concern; do not wait for a scheduled coolant-change date.

Cooling diagnosis for the 3.7L.
Cooling diagnosis for the 5.0L.

notes: Exhaust layout and replacement connections differ by engine; use the matching procedure.
guides.title: Exhaust and heat shields: follow the noise carefully
guides.summary: Inspect the hot-gas path and its protective shields as related but different parts.
guides.introduction: The exhaust directs hot gases away from the engine and occupants. Its mountings allow controlled movement, and heat shields protect nearby areas. A metallic rattle can come from a loose shield; a damaged pipe or connection is a different concern. The right inspection identifies the source instead of replacing the loudest-looking assembly.
guides.why: Loose mountings, damaged pipes and displaced shields can create noise, contact or heat exposure. Treating them as separate findings leads to a more useful repair decision.

when.summary: Inspect the exhaust and heat shields at every oil-change service. Monthly, check that any designed holes or slots in the tailpipe remain clear of debris.
notes: Only clear existing openings; do not drill new holes or change the exhaust design.

prepare.title: Allow cooling time
prepare.detail: Exhaust parts can remain hot after the engine stops.

prepare.title: Arrange underbody access
prepare.detail: Use the appropriate lifting and support procedure; do not crawl beneath a car held only by a jack.

steps.title: Describe the noise or concern
steps.body: Note whether it occurs at idle, under load, over bumps or after warm-up.

steps.title: Inspect the mounting and gas path
steps.body: Check condition and attachment of the pipes, mufflers and shields, following the engine-specific diagnosis.

steps.title: Repair the confirmed area
steps.body: Use the matching procedure and verify that the original noise or contact concern has been resolved.

watchFor.title: A loose shield
watchFor.body: Do not remove a protective shield as a permanent noise fix.

watchFor.title: Exhaust entering the cabin
watchFor.body: Treat it as a safety concern needing immediate assessment, not merely an annoyance.

Diagnose the 2.3L exhaust.
Diagnose the 3.7L exhaust.
Diagnose the 5.0L exhaust.

notes: Do not add friction modifier or substitute gear oil by habit. Differential type and the applicable specification matter.
guides.title: Rear axle inspection: look for the source of a leak
guides.summary: Inspect the rear axle and respond promptly to leakage or water exposure, without confusing inspection with an automatic fluid change.
guides.introduction: The rear differential changes the direction of drive and lets the rear wheels turn at different speeds. Its lubricant stays inside the housing, so a leak deserves attention even if the car still feels normal. An exterior inspection, a level check and a lubricant change are three different jobs.
guides.why: A low lubricant level or water contamination can compromise gears and bearings. Finding where wetness begins is more informative than ordering the nearest seal.

when.summary: Inspect the rear axle at oil-change service. Have suspected leakage or axle submersion assessed promptly.
notes: Routine fluid replacement is addressed separately because Ford’s online normal schedule and axle exception use different wording.

prepare.title: Record the event
prepare.detail: Note any wetness, new noise, repair history or water exposure.

prepare.title: Identify the assembly
prepare.detail: Confirm the axle and any cooler equipment before selecting a level-check or repair procedure.

steps.title: Look for a pattern
steps.body: Inspect the housing and surrounding areas for evidence of leakage or damage. Determine whether the observed fluid actually comes from the axle.

steps.title: Use the proper level check when needed
steps.body: A suspected leak calls for the correct inspection and fluid-level procedure, not an arbitrary top-up quantity.

steps.title: Resolve the cause
steps.body: Repair a confirmed leak or address contamination, then verify the fluid condition and level as the procedure requires.

watchFor.title: Water exposure
watchFor.body: An axle submerged in water needs prompt assessment even if there is no visible external leak.

watchFor.title: New noise with wetness
watchFor.body: Treat the observations together; do not postpone investigation until a routine service milestone.

procedures.purpose: Understand the draining and filling branches for different axle equipment.
Check differential fluid level correctly.
Diagnose rear axle and differential concerns.

notes: The driveshaft is distinct from the two rear halfshafts that connect the differential to the wheels.
guides.title: Driveshaft and U-joints: check movement, noise and mounting
guides.summary: Inspect the shaft and joints that carry drive to the rear axle; use diagnosis to separate a shaft problem from other vibration sources.
guides.introduction: The driveshaft carries torque along the car, while its joints accommodate the geometry of the drivetrain. A change in vibration, a clunk or visible damage can make this area worth inspecting. None of those symptoms alone proves that the whole shaft needs replacement.
guides.why: Joint wear, mounting issues and shaft damage affect how torque is transmitted. Tire, wheel, transmission or axle concerns can feel similar from the driver’s seat, so a good description of the symptom matters.

when.summary: Inspect at each oil-change service. Predominantly towing or car-top-carrier use calls for more frequent inspection and service as needed.
notes: Lubricate only if the fitted joint has the specified grease fitting.

prepare.title: Capture when it happens
prepare.detail: Record road speed, load, acceleration or coast conditions and whether the vibration is new.

prepare.title: Arrange safe access
prepare.detail: Underbody inspection requires correct lifting and support, with the vehicle secured as directed.

steps.title: Inspect before disturbing
steps.body: Look for damage and inspect the shaft, joints and mounting using the diagnostic procedure.

steps.title: Keep diagnosis specific
steps.body: Use the relevant runout, balance or angle checks only when the diagnosis calls for them.

steps.title: Preserve assembly requirements
steps.body: If removal is needed, follow its marking, fastening and installation instructions. Verify the original concern afterward.

watchFor.title: A new vibration after other work
watchFor.body: Include installation and mounting history in the investigation.

watchFor.title: A joint with no grease fitting
watchFor.body: Do not invent a lubrication point or assume all joints are serviced the same way.

procedures.purpose: Follow driveshaft removal and installation.
Diagnose a driveshaft concern.
Use runout and balancing checks when indicated.
Service the driveshaft universal joint when applicable.

notes: Avoid treating a boot as a periodic oil-fill point. Halfshaft-joint grease and differential lubricant have different jobs.
guides.title: Halfshaft boots: protect the joint before dirt gets in
guides.summary: Look for damaged boots and escaping grease around the rear drive halfshafts.
guides.introduction: Each rear halfshaft carries drive from the differential to a wheel. Its flexible boots help keep joint grease inside while excluding water and road grit. The boot is not decoration: a damaged one changes the environment in which the joint works.
guides.why: A boot can be damaged before the joint becomes noisy. Catching that change early creates a better opportunity to assess the joint’s condition instead of waiting for an obvious driveline symptom.

when.summary: Inspect the halfshaft boots at every oil-change service; investigate visible grease loss sooner.

prepare.title: Locate both sides
prepare.detail: The left and right halfshafts each need attention; inspect the accessible boot surfaces rather than just the most visible outer joint.

prepare.title: Use proper access
prepare.detail: Do not work beneath a car held only by a jack.

steps.title: Inspect the flexible covers
steps.body: Look for visible damage, displaced attachment and grease escaping around the boot or nearby surfaces.

steps.title: Identify the affected area
steps.body: Distinguish boot grease from an axle-seal leak. The source determines which procedure is useful.

steps.title: Have the joint assessed
steps.body: A damaged boot needs a repair decision based on contamination, joint condition and the available service procedure.

watchFor.title: Grease thrown onto surrounding parts
watchFor.body: Trace it back to its origin rather than simply cleaning it away.

watchFor.title: Noise or vibration
watchFor.body: Include the boot finding in diagnosis, but do not assume it proves the joint is the only cause.

procedures.purpose: See the rear halfshaft arrangement and repair procedure.
Diagnose rear halfshaft concerns.
Use the axle-seal procedure if the leak originates at that seal.

notes: Lubricate only a specified grease fitting where one is fitted. Do not generalize that instruction to boots or dry rubber bushings.
guides.title: Steering linkage: inspect the mechanical connection
guides.summary: Check the linkage and joints; the electric steering system has no hydraulic reservoir to top up.
guides.introduction: The steering gear moves the tie rods, which change the direction of the front wheels. Electric assistance reduces the effort at the steering wheel, but the mechanical joints still need to hold their geometry. A useful check considers looseness, damage and changing steering behavior rather than looking for a power-steering fluid service.
guides.why: A worn joint can allow wheel movement that was not requested at the steering wheel. Tire and suspension concerns can also affect steering feel, so diagnosis needs to consider the whole front end.

when.summary: Inspect steering linkage, ball joints and tie-rod ends at each oil-change service.
notes: The electric-assist system has no power-steering-fluid reservoir, top-up or flush interval.

prepare.title: Describe the feel
prepare.detail: Record a new pull, looseness, stiffness or knock and the conditions in which it occurs.

prepare.title: Confirm the exact component
prepare.detail: The steering column, steering gear and tie rods are related parts with different procedures.

steps.title: Inspect the mechanical system
steps.body: Check the linkage and joints according to the steering and suspension diagnostic instructions.

steps.title: Separate mechanical and assist concerns
steps.body: A warning or a change in electric assistance needs the power-steering diagnostic path; a suspected worn joint needs mechanical assessment.

steps.title: Verify the repair
steps.body: Use the correct replacement and alignment-related instructions, then confirm the original concern is resolved.

watchFor.title: A steering warning or marked change in effort
watchFor.body: Have the system assessed rather than looking for fluid to add.

watchFor.title: Play or damaged joint protection
watchFor.body: Identify the affected joint before ordering a gear assembly.

Service the inner tie rod.
Follow power-steering diagnosis.
Understand electric steering operation.

notes: Suspension inspection is not permission to grease all bushings. Stabilizer-bar bushing care has a specific dry-installation rule.
guides.title: Suspension checks: follow wear, leaks and ride changes
guides.summary: Inspect arms, joints, springs, dampers and mountings as a connected system.
guides.introduction: The suspension keeps the tire controlled as the road and vehicle loads change. Arms locate the wheel, springs carry load and dampers control movement. Bushings and joints let the system move without losing its intended geometry. That is why a single clunk or uneven tire-wear pattern can have several possible causes.
guides.why: A worn mounting can make a good damper or arm seem faulty. Looking across the system helps connect a symptom to an actual finding.

when.summary: Inspect at each oil-change service. Investigate a new knock, unstable feeling, ride-height change or visible damage sooner.

prepare.title: Start with the basics
prepare.detail: Check tire pressure, approved tire size and loading before treating the suspension as the cause.

prepare.title: Record modifications
prepare.detail: Aftermarket springs, arms, wheels or other changes can affect which specifications apply.

steps.title: Describe and reproduce the concern safely
steps.body: Note road surface, speed and loading. Use the diagnostic path for the symptom rather than a guessed replacement list.

steps.title: Inspect component condition
steps.body: Check the arms, joints, bushings, dampers and fasteners for the wear, damage or leakage called out by diagnosis.

steps.title: Repair and verify
steps.body: Complete the correct component procedure and any required alignment checks. Confirm the car behaves as expected afterward.

watchFor.title: A recurring alignment complaint
watchFor.body: Worn or damaged parts need attention before an alignment can be relied on.

watchFor.title: Oil around a damper or visible damage
watchFor.body: Have the condition assessed; do not assign a universal replacement mileage to every shock or strut.

guides.title: Stabilizer bushings: inspect them, keep them dry
guides.summary: Understand the no-lubrication rule, the front performance-package restriction and the different front/rear installation details.
guides.introduction: A stabilizer bar links the suspension’s response from side to side, helping resist body roll. Its support bushings hold the bar in its brackets while allowing its intended movement. When a clunk appears, these bushings are worth inspecting, but the links, brackets and other suspension joints can make similar noises.
guides.why: The specified rubber bushing design works without applied lubricant. Greasing it as a noise shortcut can damage it and leave the actual source of the clunk unresolved.

when.summary: Inspect with the suspension at oil service, or sooner when a clunk, loose handling or visible damage appears. Replace after inspection confirms a defect.
notes: There is no automatic mileage-based bushing replacement in this schedule.

prepare.title: Identify front or rear
prepare.detail: The installation details are not the same at both ends of the car.

prepare.title: Confirm the front package
prepare.detail: On performance-package vehicles, the front bushings are not serviced separately; replacement uses the front bar assembly.

steps.title: Locate the actual concern
steps.body: Inspect the bushing, bracket, bar and links with the suspension diagnosis in mind. Do not diagnose by sound alone.

steps.title: Choose the right repair branch
steps.body: Use the front or rear procedure and the appropriate engine/equipment access instructions.

steps.title: Keep installation details intact
steps.body: Use new bracket bolts and the specified slit orientation. Front slits face rearward; rear slits face forward.

watchFor.title: A proposed grease cure
watchFor.body: Do not lubricate the stabilizer bar or bushings.

watchFor.title: A separately advertised front bushing
watchFor.body: Confirm whether the fitted performance-package bar allows that service.

Follow rear bushing orientation and bracket instructions.
Investigate the suspension noise before selecting parts.

notes: This guide is for the 6R80 automatic, not the MT82 or 3160 manual transmission.
guides.title: 6R80 fluid level: this is a measured workshop check
guides.summary: Understand why temperature, the level indicator and the checking procedure matter more than an assumed fill amount.
guides.introduction: Automatic-transmission fluid changes volume with temperature and circulates through more than the pan. On the 6R80, the level-check procedure uses a diagnostic scan tool, a specific temperature range and the transmission’s level indicator. It is not the same quick check as pulling the engine-oil dipstick.
guides.why: Too little fluid can damage the transmission, and overfilling is not a safe workaround. A correct reading depends on following the specified operating and temperature conditions.

when.summary: The normal oil-service checklist includes transmission level inspection where applicable; use the 6R80-specific procedure to determine and perform the correct check.
notes: Investigate suspected leakage or a shift concern separately. This does not replace the fluid-and-filter replacement interval.

prepare.title: Have the required capability
prepare.detail: Plan for a scan tool that reads transmission fluid temperature and safe access on a level, properly supported vehicle.

prepare.title: Read the full procedure first
prepare.detail: The check involves an operating engine and hot components; the sequence and temperature window are essential.

steps.title: Establish the specified conditions
steps.body: Follow the procedure’s gear-selection and temperature preparation rather than checking at an arbitrary cold or hot condition.

steps.title: Use the correct indicator markings
steps.body: The procedure identifies the dotted area to use. Confirm the reading using that instruction.

steps.title: Correct and verify
steps.body: If needed, add or remove the specified fluid through the correct procedure, then recheck and complete the closure steps.

watchFor.title: A confirmed low level
watchFor.body: The procedure says not to drive with low transmission fluid; arrange correction and investigate the cause.

watchFor.title: A refill based only on capacity
watchFor.body: Dry capacity and a service refill are different quantities. Finish by the specified level check.

procedures.purpose: Perform the exact 6R80 temperature-controlled level check.
Add or remove fluid using the drain/refill procedure.

notes: The cabin filter and engine air filter have different service intervals and are not interchangeable parts.
guides.title: Cabin air filter: restore a clean airflow path
guides.summary: Replace the filter serving cabin ventilation and distinguish it from an engine air filter or an A/C repair.
guides.introduction: Air entering the heating and air-conditioning system passes through a cabin filter. As the element collects dust, it can become a restriction. Replacing it is a focused service job: it does not require replacing the blower motor, and it does not fix every reason the cabin air may feel weak or warm.
guides.why: A clean, correctly fitted element helps the ventilation system move air without drawing around a poorly seated filter. Its job is different from refrigerant cooling or temperature-door control.

when.summary: Replace every 20,000 mi (32,000 km) in normal use.
notes: Dusty conditions can require earlier inspection and replacement. Frequent inspection is also called for with extensive low-speed commercial use.

prepare.title: Get the correct element
prepare.detail: Confirm the replacement’s application and any orientation markings.

prepare.title: Prepare the passenger-side access
prepare.detail: The linked procedure accesses the filter through the right lower instrument-panel area.

steps.title: Open the access area
steps.body: Follow the retainer and lower-insulator removal instructions, then remove the filter cover.

steps.title: Change the element
steps.body: Remove the old cabin filter and install the correct replacement with its intended orientation and fit.

steps.title: Close and verify
steps.body: Refit the cover and insulator securely, then check normal ventilation operation.

watchFor.title: A poor fit or damaged cover
watchFor.body: Air needs to pass through the element, not around an incorrectly fitted one.

watchFor.title: Airflow that remains poor
watchFor.body: A clean filter is one check; continue diagnosis if the symptom remains.

procedures.purpose: Follow the complete cabin-filter access and installation steps.

notes: The linked air-cleaner procedures cover complete assembly access. Routine element service does not automatically require every full-assembly removal operation.
guides.title: Engine air filter: change the element, protect the intake
guides.summary: Keep incoming dirt out while preserving the correct seal and duct connections for your engine.
guides.introduction: The engine needs air, but abrasive dirt should stay on the dirty side of the air-filter element. The housing, element and connected ducting form one path. A fresh element helps only if it sits correctly and the housing is closed as intended.
guides.why: A damaged, poorly seated or heavily loaded element changes how the intake is protected. The air-cleaner housing is normally a reusable assembly; the scheduled replacement item is the filter element.

when.summary: Replace the element every 30,000 mi (48,000 km) in normal use.
notes: Predominantly dusty or sandy use: inspect at 15,000 mi (24,000 km) and replace as needed.

prepare.title: Identify the engine and element
prepare.detail: The 2.3L, 3.7L and 5.0L air-cleaner arrangements differ.

prepare.title: Keep the clean side clean
prepare.detail: Prepare a clean work area so debris is not introduced while the housing is open.

steps.title: Access the correct housing
steps.body: Use the engine-specific air-cleaner instructions to understand the clips, connections and cover arrangement.

steps.title: Inspect and replace the element
steps.body: Check the removed element and its seating area; install the correct new element securely.

steps.title: Restore the intake path
steps.body: Close the housing and verify any connections disturbed during access. Avoid leaving an opening or poorly seated duct.

watchFor.title: An element that does not sit naturally
watchFor.body: Recheck the part and orientation rather than forcing the cover closed.

watchFor.title: An ongoing performance concern
watchFor.body: Replacing a dirty filter is maintenance; a remaining symptom still needs diagnosis.
