3.7L air-cleaner arrangement and access.
5.0L air-cleaner arrangement and access.

notes: These time and mileage intervals are for the stated 2015 base engines. They do not establish a 5.2L schedule.
guides.title: Coolant replacement: fluid choice and trapped air matter
guides.summary: Refresh the coolant at its time-or-distance deadline and use the correct filling and bleeding process.
guides.introduction: Coolant carries heat and helps protect the cooling system’s internal surfaces. A replacement renews the fluid, but the job is not finished merely because the reservoir looks full. The system also needs the specified concentration and a filling method that removes trapped air.
guides.why: Air pockets and incorrect coolant can undermine an otherwise sound cooling system. The correct procedure is as important as choosing the bottle with the right specification.

when.summary: First replacement: six years or 100,000 mi (160,000 km). Afterward: every three years or 50,000 mi (80,000 km), whichever comes first.
notes: Use elapsed time from the actual replacement when planning the next service.

prepare.title: Let the engine cool
prepare.detail: Opening a hot pressurized cooling system can cause serious burns.

prepare.title: Gather the specified fluid and equipment
prepare.detail: Read the engine-specific draining, vacuum-filling and bleeding instructions before starting. Arrange collection and proper disposal of old coolant.

steps.title: Confirm the service history and fluid
steps.body: Identify what is due and use the required coolant for the engine.

steps.title: Drain and refill by the correct procedure
steps.body: Follow its access, draining, filling-equipment and bleeding requirements in order.

steps.title: Complete the final checks
steps.body: Verify the final level and absence of leaks as directed, then record the date, mileage and coolant used.

watchFor.title: Repeated coolant loss
watchFor.body: Find and repair the cause; a scheduled fluid replacement is not a leak repair.

watchFor.title: Unstable temperature after service
watchFor.body: Stop and assess the filling/bleeding result rather than assuming the new coolant solved the issue.

procedures.purpose: 2.3L draining, vacuum filling and bleeding.
3.7L draining, vacuum filling and bleeding.
5.0L draining, vacuum filling and bleeding.

notes: Choose the plug procedure that matches your engine.
guides.title: Spark plugs: renew a wear item without guessing at a misfire
guides.summary: Use the engine-specific plug and installation procedure, and keep scheduled replacement separate from fault diagnosis.
guides.introduction: A spark plug repeatedly starts combustion by making a spark across its electrodes. Those electrodes wear with use, which makes plugs a scheduled service item. An ignition coil has a different job and does not automatically need replacement when the plugs are due.
guides.why: The correct plug type and installation protect both ignition performance and the cylinder-head threads. A rough-running engine can also have fuel or mechanical causes, so fresh plugs are not a substitute for diagnosis.

when.summary: Replace every 100,000 mi (160,000 km) in normal use.
notes: Predominantly towing/car-top-carrier use or extensive idling/low-speed commercial use: 60,000 mi (96,000 km).

prepare.title: Confirm the engine and plug
prepare.detail: Use the correct part and specified installation information for the 2.3L, 3.7L or 5.0L.

prepare.title: Review access before starting
prepare.detail: The coil and surrounding-component access differs by engine. Keep debris away from open plug holes.

steps.title: Follow the engine’s access sequence
steps.body: Remove the required components in the prescribed order rather than borrowing another engine’s shortcut.

steps.title: Replace the plugs correctly
steps.body: Use the specified plug and tightening method. Do not invent a universal torque or assume an installation compound is required.

steps.title: Reassemble and verify
steps.body: Restore coils and connections, then check normal operation. Record the service mileage.

watchFor.title: A misfire that remains
watchFor.body: Continue diagnosis instead of repeatedly replacing ignition parts.

watchFor.title: Unexpected damage or contamination
watchFor.body: A removed plug can provide evidence of another concern; retain that information for diagnosis.

procedures.purpose: Replace 2.3L spark plugs.
Replace 3.7L spark plugs.
Replace 5.0L spark plugs.

notes: The belt interval does not automatically require new pulleys or tensioners. Use the belt routing for the selected engine.
guides.title: Accessory belts: inspect the belt and the system driving it
guides.summary: Follow the belt inspection and replacement cadence, while keeping pulley and tensioner diagnosis separate.
guides.introduction: An accessory belt transfers crankshaft rotation to its driven accessories. Its routing, the way tension is controlled and any separate A/C belt depend on the engine. Knowing that layout helps you distinguish belt wear from a pulley, tensioner or installation problem.
guides.why: A belt may deteriorate with age or contamination, but noise alone does not identify the failed part. Replacing a tensioner on a mileage schedule intended for the belt can add work without addressing the cause.

when.summary: Inspect at 100,000 mi (160,000 km), then every other oil change until replacement. Replace the belts at 150,000 mi (240,000 km).
notes: Inspect sooner if there is damage, contamination or a new noise.

prepare.title: Identify the belt arrangement
prepare.detail: Use the correct engine diagram, including a separate A/C belt where fitted.

prepare.title: Plan for safe access
prepare.detail: Inspect with the engine off. Read the removal and installation method before releasing tension or removing a belt.

steps.title: Review belt condition and routing
steps.body: Check for contamination, incorrect seating and visible deterioration using the relevant accessory-drive diagnosis.

steps.title: Investigate the cause of abnormal wear
steps.body: A damaged or misaligned pulley can affect a replacement belt too. Check the system when the evidence calls for it.

steps.title: Replace and verify by engine
steps.body: Follow the correct installation sequence and routing, then complete its operation checks.

watchFor.title: A proposed lubricant or belt dressing
watchFor.body: Do not lubricate the accessory belt.

watchFor.title: Cracks versus actual damage
watchFor.body: The 2.3L diagnostic guidance distinguishes small cracks from exposed cord or missing chunks; apply the relevant engine’s inspection criteria.

procedures.purpose: Replace the 2.3L accessory belt.
Replace the 3.7L accessory belt.
Replace the 5.0L accessory belt.
Use the 2.3L accessory-drive condition checks.

notes: Do not substitute a generic transmission flush or additive routine for the specified service.
guides.title: 6R80 automatic fluid and filter service
guides.summary: Plan the filter work and the fluid work together, then finish with the specified level check.
guides.introduction: The 6R80 uses its fluid for lubrication and hydraulic operation. The scheduled service includes both fluid and filter, so a simple drain/refill and a complete filter service are not identical jobs. Read the linked procedures together before deciding what equipment and parts are needed.
guides.why: Correct fluid, cleanliness and final level are essential. A refill based on a guessed capacity can leave the transmission underfilled or overfilled even though fluid was added.

when.summary: Change automatic-transmission fluid and filter every 150,000 mi (240,000 km) in normal use.
notes: A leak, contamination concern or diagnosed fault can require service earlier.

prepare.title: Verify 6R80 fitment
prepare.detail: This guide does not apply to an MT82 or 3160 manual gearbox.

prepare.title: Prepare for the final check
prepare.detail: Have the specified fluid, appropriate filter/pan parts, safe access and the scan-tool capability needed to verify fluid temperature.

steps.title: Read the related procedures as one plan
steps.body: Review pan/filter access, draining/refilling and level checking before opening the system.

steps.title: Keep the work clean
steps.body: Perform the required fluid and filter operations with the specified materials and component instructions.

steps.title: Set the level and verify
steps.body: Finish using the exact temperature-controlled level procedure. Check the serviced area and confirm operation before recording the job as complete.

watchFor.title: Low fluid or shift concerns
watchFor.body: Diagnose the cause; changing fluid does not prove an internal fault has been repaired.

watchFor.title: A quoted “capacity” used as the only endpoint
watchFor.body: A dry fill and the amount required after a service operation are different. Use the level procedure.

procedures.purpose: Service the transmission pan, gasket and filter.
Drain and refill the 6R80.
Complete the temperature-controlled fluid-level check.

notes: Do not transfer these intervals or fluid instructions to the 3160 or to an automatic transmission.
guides.title: MT82 manual transmission fluid: use the gearbox specification
guides.summary: Renew the lubricant in the manual gearbox without confusing it with automatic-transmission or differential oil.
guides.introduction: The manual gearbox’s oil lubricates its gears and bearings while working with the synchronizers used during gear changes. “Transmission fluid” is therefore not one universal product. The MT82 procedure and specification determine what belongs in this gearbox.
guides.why: The correct lubricant supports both protection and shift operation. A hard shift can have several causes, so a fluid service is not a guaranteed cure for a clutch or gearbox fault.

when.summary: Every 150,000 mi (240,000 km) in normal use.
notes: Predominantly towing/car-top-carrier use: 60,000 mi (96,000 km).
Predominantly dusty or sandy driving: 50,000 mi (80,000 km).

prepare.title: Confirm the transmission
prepare.detail: These instructions are for the MT82, not the 5.2L’s 3160 gearbox.

prepare.title: Plan a level vehicle and fluid delivery
prepare.detail: The procedure requires a level vehicle and suitable equipment to fill the transmission.

steps.title: Verify the lubricant requirement
steps.body: Use the MT82 specification rather than choosing oil by a generic viscosity label alone.

steps.title: Drain and fill in sequence
steps.body: Follow the prescribed drain, fill and closure operations, using the exact fastener requirements from the linked article.

steps.title: Check the result
steps.body: Verify the final level as directed, look for leakage and record the date, mileage and lubricant used.

watchFor.title: A recurring leak
watchFor.body: Address its source instead of treating repeated top-ups as maintenance.

watchFor.title: A shift problem that continues
watchFor.body: Follow diagnosis; fresh fluid does not establish that the clutch or synchronizers are sound.

procedures.purpose: Drain and fill the MT82.
Check MT82 fluid level.
Confirm the MT82 lubricant and specifications.

notes: Confirm the vehicle-specific instruction before booking routine axle-fluid replacement. Suspected leakage or submersion needs attention regardless of the odometer.
guides.title: Rear axle fluid: confirm the schedule and the differential type
guides.summary: Understand Ford’s 150,000-mile normal-schedule entry and the separately stated axle exception before choosing a service deadline.
guides.introduction: Rear axle lubricant protects the gears and bearings inside the differential. Choosing the right service requires two pieces of information: the fitted differential and the maintenance instruction that applies to the car’s use. The drain/fill procedure also has branches for different equipment, including whether a drain plug or cooler is fitted.
guides.why: A gear-oil choice, friction-modifier instruction or filling method from another axle can be wrong for this one. Confirming the assembly first avoids turning a routine fluid job into an experiment.

when.summary: The normal schedule lists rear axle fluid replacement at 150,000 mi (240,000 km); read the axle exception before treating that as an unconditional deadline.
notes: Ford’s special-conditions page separately says axle fluid checks or changes are not required unless leakage is suspected or the assembly has been submerged. These online instructions need to be reconciled for the vehicle’s applicable schedule.
Suspected leakage or submersion needs prompt assessment regardless of mileage.

prepare.title: Identify the axle and equipment
prepare.detail: Confirm the differential type and whether a cooler is fitted.

prepare.title: Confirm the applicable service plan
prepare.detail: Review the normal entry together with the exception and the vehicle’s original maintenance information; obtain a vehicle-specific recommendation if they differ.

steps.title: Resolve the service scope
steps.body: Decide whether this is routine replacement, a leak repair or contamination after water exposure.

steps.title: Use the correct equipment branch
steps.body: Follow the draining/filling procedure for the actual axle, with its specified lubricant and any applicable additive.

steps.title: Finish with the correct level
steps.body: Complete the specified fill, closure and leak checks, and record what fluid and service were used.

watchFor.title: Water exposure or leaking seals
watchFor.body: Do not delay assessment because a mileage milestone is far away.

watchFor.title: Additive used by habit
watchFor.body: A limited-slip label alone is not a substitute for the exact application instructions.

procedures.purpose: Use the axle-equipment branches for draining and filling.
Check differential fluid level.
Confirm the axle lubricant specifications.

notes: Do not bridge the battery terminals with tools. A replacement decision should follow the condition assessment.
guides.title: Battery connections: check the path before replacing the battery
guides.summary: Inspect connections and assess battery condition when starting performance changes.
guides.introduction: Starting demands a strong electrical path as well as a charged battery. Corrosion, a poor connection or a cable problem can interfere with that path. A regular connection check is useful maintenance; replacing the battery on a guessed calendar interval is a different decision.
guides.why: A weak-start symptom can involve the battery, charging system, cables or an electrical drain. Looking at connections first gives diagnosis better evidence.

when.summary: Check battery connections every six months and clean as needed. Battery performance is part of the recommended multi-point inspection.

prepare.title: Review battery precautions
prepare.detail: Keep sparks and ignition sources away and use the appropriate personal protection.

prepare.title: Read the disconnect procedure before cleaning work
prepare.detail: A task that requires disconnection needs the correct sequence and any post-connection considerations.

steps.title: Inspect the connections
steps.body: Look for an obvious connection problem or corrosion and assess what work is actually needed.

steps.title: Clean or correct safely
steps.body: Use the specified battery procedure rather than disturbing terminals with the electrical system in an inappropriate state.

steps.title: Verify starting and charging as needed
steps.body: If the concern remains, test the battery and related system instead of assuming that cleaning proves the battery is healthy.

watchFor.title: A repeat low-charge condition
watchFor.body: Include charging performance and possible drains in diagnosis.

watchFor.title: Changes after disconnection
watchFor.body: The vehicle may need to relearn adaptive behavior; follow the reconnection guidance rather than immediately replacing unrelated parts.

procedures.purpose: Service the battery and its mounting.
Disconnect and reconnect correctly.
Use the battery-charging procedure.
Investigate an abnormal electrical drain.

notes: Follow the precautions for the fitted lighting technology. Do not improvise powered tests at lamp connectors.
guides.title: Lighting checks: make sure the car can see and be seen
guides.summary: Check interior and exterior lamp operation and diagnose the correct circuit before ordering a lamp.
guides.introduction: A lighting check is quick, but it should be deliberate. Headlamps, signaling lamps and interior lights do different jobs. A failed lamp, a control setting and a wiring issue can all present as “the light does not work,” so record exactly which function is missing.
guides.why: Lighting supports visibility and communicates with other road users. A bulb change will not correct a fault in its supply, ground or control circuit.

when.summary: Check interior and exterior light operation monthly; include hazard-warning and horn operation in the recommended service inspection.

prepare.title: Choose a safe place
prepare.detail: Park securely and arrange a helper or a safe viewing method for lamps that are difficult to observe from the controls.

prepare.title: Know the fitted lamp type
prepare.detail: Replacement methods differ for bulbs, complete assemblies and high-intensity lighting equipment.

steps.title: Work through the functions
steps.body: Operate the lighting controls and check the corresponding lamps rather than checking only the headlamps.

steps.title: Record a specific failure
steps.body: Note the side, lamp, function and whether it is intermittent.

steps.title: Use the matching repair path
steps.body: Follow diagnosis if needed, then use the correct bulb or assembly procedure and verify operation afterward.

watchFor.title: Several functions fail together
watchFor.body: Look for a shared electrical cause rather than ordering several lamps at once.

watchFor.title: A lamp works but points incorrectly
watchFor.body: Aim is a separate check from simply illuminating.

procedures.purpose: Service the headlamp assembly when required.
Use the headlamp-bulb procedure for applicable equipment.
Check and adjust headlamp aim.
Diagnose headlamp operation.

notes: The illustrated motor/linkage is background context. Routine blade care does not require removing that assembly.
guides.title: Washers and wipers: keep the complete cleaning system working
guides.summary: Check fluid, spray and blade performance as connected but separate jobs.
guides.introduction: The washers loosen and carry dirt, while the blades clear the glass. Weak spray and poor wiping can happen together, but they do not necessarily have the same cause. Start with the fluid and visible condition before deciding that the motor or linkage needs replacement.
guides.why: Good visibility depends on the system working as a whole. A new wiper motor cannot correct an empty washer reservoir or a worn blade edge.

when.summary: Check washer-fluid level monthly. Check spray and wiper operation every six months; clean or replace blades as needed.

prepare.title: Use the appropriate washer fluid
prepare.detail: Choose a product suitable for the expected temperatures and vehicle requirements.

prepare.title: Inspect the glass and blades
prepare.detail: A dirty windshield or contaminated blade can affect the result of an operation check.

steps.title: Check the supply
steps.body: Confirm washer-fluid level and look for an obvious leak if the level repeatedly falls.

steps.title: Check spray and wiping
steps.body: Verify that fluid reaches the glass and that the blades clear it properly.

steps.title: Address the actual finding
steps.body: Clean or replace blades when needed. Use washer or wiper diagnosis for continuing spray, motor or linkage concerns.

watchFor.title: Continuing streaks or missed areas
watchFor.body: Inspect blade and glass condition before blaming the motor.

watchFor.title: A pump runs but fluid does not arrive
watchFor.body: Investigate the fluid path rather than assuming the motor is the only serviceable part.

procedures.purpose: Understand the wiper and washer system.
Diagnose continuing operating concerns.
Locate and service the washer reservoir if required.
Use the motor procedure only when that repair is needed.

notes: The door-removal link is for structural context or a confirmed repair, not a routine drain-cleaning step. Convertible roof seals have their own procedures.
guides.title: Body drains and weather seals: give water a way out
guides.summary: Check drainage openings and seal condition without disturbing the door or packing drain paths with products.
guides.introduction: Weather seals help manage water and wind around body openings, while designed drain holes let water escape from areas where it can collect. Both deserve attention. A wet interior does not automatically prove that the nearest weatherstrip is the failed part.
guides.why: An obstructed drain and a damaged seal create different problems and need different responses. Regular checks can reveal debris or visible wear before water is left trapped in an enclosed area.

when.summary: Every six months: check body and door drains for obstruction and door weatherstrips for wear; clean or lubricate as appropriate.
notes: Use the correct care product and application instructions for the specific seal.

prepare.title: Locate the intended openings
prepare.detail: Identify actual drainage features; do not create holes or enlarge an opening to guess at a water path.

prepare.title: Inspect before adding products
prepare.detail: Look for debris, wear and displaced seals before deciding that lubrication is the answer.

steps.title: Check the drain paths
steps.body: Look for obstruction in the designed body and door drain openings and clean as needed without damaging surrounding finishes.

steps.title: Inspect seals
steps.body: Review visible weatherstrip condition and seating. Use the approved care instructions if lubrication is needed.

steps.title: Investigate continuing water entry
steps.body: Record where and when water appears and have its path identified before replacing trim or seals.

watchFor.title: Repeated dampness
watchFor.body: The entry point can differ from where water collects. Keep observations for diagnosis.

watchFor.title: A seal displaced by another problem
watchFor.body: Door alignment or damage may need assessment rather than simply forcing the seal back into place.

procedures.purpose: Understand the front-door assembly before any confirmed door repair.
Assess door alignment when fit is part of the concern.
Review corrosion-prevention requirements after body work.

notes: Keep fingers clear of moving latch parts. A lubrication procedure does not mean the whole latch assembly needs replacement.
guides.title: Hinges, latches and locks: smooth operation without excess grease
guides.summary: Check engagement and release, then lubricate the mechanism only where the procedure specifies.
guides.introduction: A latch should engage securely and release when commanded. Hinges, check arms, external locks and latch mechanisms do different jobs, even though they are used together whenever a door opens. A sticking door needs its cause identified before a lubricant is sprayed into every nearby opening.
guides.why: Correct lubrication can support operation, but excess product can reach places where it causes trouble. The door-latch procedure specifically warns that over-lubrication can damage the internal lock motor.

when.summary: Check operation every six months and lubricate where needed using the applicable procedure.
notes: Address failure to latch or release promptly.

prepare.title: Identify the mechanism
prepare.detail: Separate a hinge or alignment concern from a latch, external lock or electrical-control concern.

prepare.title: Choose the specified product
prepare.detail: Use the procedure’s material and application point instead of a general-purpose spray chosen by habit.

steps.title: Check normal movement
steps.body: Observe whether the mechanism binds, fails to engage or requires unusual effort.

steps.title: Perform targeted lubrication if needed
steps.body: Follow the latch procedure’s positioning, application and release sequence. Do not over-lubricate.

steps.title: Verify full operation
steps.body: Check that the latch is released before closing and that it then engages and opens correctly.

watchFor.title: A door that needs slamming
watchFor.body: Have fit and latch operation assessed rather than accepting extra force as normal.

watchFor.title: Intermittent electric locking
watchFor.body: Lubrication is not a substitute for diagnosis of an electrical or motor fault.

procedures.purpose: Follow the exact door-latch lubrication sequence.
Service the front-door latch when repair is necessary.
Diagnose locks, latches and entry-system concerns.

notes: Do not use this inspection as permission to probe, power or dismantle a pretensioner. Restraint repairs have dedicated safety requirements.
guides.title: Seatbelts and seat latches: check the parts you rely on
guides.summary: Inspect wear and function, and keep routine checks separate from the inspection required after a collision.
guides.introduction: The seatbelt’s webbing, buckle, retractor and anchorages work together to restrain an occupant. Seat latches must also hold their intended position. A routine check should look beyond whether the buckle clicks: the complete assembly needs to remain in good condition.
guides.why: Damage to one part can compromise the whole restraint path. A belt that appears to operate normally after a collision has not thereby passed the required post-collision inspection.

when.summary: Check seatbelts and seat latches for wear and proper function every six months.
notes: Collision repair requires the separate inspection of all seatbelt components.

prepare.title: Inspect every seating position
prepare.detail: Do not limit the check to the belt used most often.

prepare.title: Keep cleaning appropriate
prepare.detail: Use the recommended cleaning method; do not bleach or re-dye seatbelt webbing.

steps.title: Review visible condition
steps.body: Inspect accessible webbing and components for damage, and confirm that belt routing is correct.

steps.title: Check operation
steps.body: Check buckle, retractor and seat-latch function using the appropriate inspection procedure.

steps.title: Escalate a defect or collision history
steps.body: Use the dedicated restraint diagnosis or post-collision procedure. Replacement must include the prescribed checks, not simply bolting in a part.

watchFor.title: Frayed, damaged or twisted webbing
watchFor.body: Have the condition assessed; do not conceal it with a cover or chemical treatment.

watchFor.title: A latch that does not engage reliably
watchFor.body: Address it before relying on that seating position.

procedures.purpose: Perform seatbelt maintenance inspection.
Follow the belt-cleaning precautions.
Use the required post-collision procedure.
Understand the front retractor/pretensioner assembly.
Service a confirmed rear seat-backrest latch concern.

notes: The cluster can display warnings from other modules. Replacing the display is not the default response to an active warning.
guides.title: Warning lamps: know a check from an active warning
guides.summary: Check that safety indicators work and respond to the actual message instead of merely clearing it.
guides.introduction: Warning lamps and messages are part of the car’s conversation with you. An indicator’s normal start-up behavior differs from a warning that remains on or appears while driving. Checking operation is useful maintenance; interpreting an active warning requires the meaning of that exact lamp or message.
guides.why: A working warning system can alert you to a developing problem. Clearing a code or turning a reminder off does not repair the system that produced it.

when.summary: Check operation of brake, ABS, airbag and seatbelt warning lamps every six months.
notes: Respond to an active warning when it occurs; do not wait for the routine check.

prepare.title: Know the expected behavior
prepare.detail: Use the information-display and system descriptions for the actual fitted cluster.

prepare.title: Record the exact message
prepare.detail: A photograph taken while safely parked can help preserve wording and conditions for diagnosis.

steps.title: Observe normal start-up indications
steps.body: Compare the lamp behavior with the described operation rather than assuming every illuminated lamp is a fault.

steps.title: Act on a continuing warning
steps.body: Follow the action associated with that exact message. Do not treat a brake-system warning as an oil-service reminder.

steps.title: Diagnose before clearing
steps.body: Use the relevant system’s tests to find the reason, then verify that the warning behaves normally after repair.

watchFor.title: Low engine oil pressure
watchFor.body: Stop safely and turn off the engine; check the level and obtain assistance if the warning persists.

watchFor.title: Check Brake System or low brake fluid
watchFor.body: Stop safely and arrange prompt brake-system assessment.

procedures.purpose: Understand cluster indicators and message operation.
Diagnose instrumentation and message concerns.
Follow brake-system diagnosis.

notes: Brake fluid can damage paint. The master-cylinder procedure requires spilled fluid on paintwork to be washed off immediately with cold water.
The linked master-cylinder replacement article is repair context; removal is not part of checking the reservoir level.
guides.title: Brake and clutch fluid: check the level without masking the problem
guides.summary: Understand the reservoir’s normal range and why an out-of-range level needs assessment.
guides.introduction: Brake fluid transmits force through the hydraulic system. On manual-transmission cars, the clutch hydraulic supply is also associated with this reservoir. A level check is simple, but a low reading should lead to an explanation rather than repeated topping up without diagnosis.
guides.why: Fluid loss, brake condition and hydraulic faults have different implications. Keeping dirt or the wrong fluid out is important whenever the reservoir or system is serviced.

when.summary: Check fluid level as part of the recommended multi-point inspection at scheduled service, and respond immediately to a low-fluid warning.
notes: This guide does not assign a blanket calendar replacement interval not stated by the reviewed 2015 schedule.

prepare.title: Identify the reservoir
prepare.detail: Confirm the brake-fluid reservoir and its MIN/MAX markings before adding anything.

prepare.title: Keep the system clean
prepare.detail: Use the exact specified fluid if service calls for it; do not introduce dirt or petroleum products.

steps.title: Read the marked range
steps.body: Ford describes a level between MIN and MAX as normal, with no addition needed.

steps.title: Respond to an abnormal reading
steps.body: If the level is outside the normal range, arrange immediate service rather than treating an arbitrary top-up as the repair.

steps.title: Use the correct hydraulic procedure
steps.body: If work opens the system, complete the applicable filling/bleeding and verification operations before relying on normal braking.

watchFor.title: A repeated level drop
watchFor.body: Have the reason investigated instead of repeatedly filling the reservoir.

watchFor.title: Changed pedal behavior or a brake warning
watchFor.body: Treat it as an active braking concern, not routine maintenance to postpone.

procedures.purpose: Identify the master-cylinder/reservoir assembly and its service precautions.
Diagnose an abnormal level or braking symptom.
Use the brake-pressure bleeding procedure when required by the repair.

guides.title: Pressure-bleed the brake hydraulic system
guides.summary: Remove air after hydraulic repairs, with the correct fluid, pressure equipment and wheel sequence. Includes the extra steps for a new ABS hydraulic unit.
guides.introduction: The brake pedal sends force through fluid to the calipers. Air compresses much more readily than brake fluid, so trapped air can use up pedal travel before the pads clamp firmly. Pressure bleeding feeds clean fluid into the reservoir and carries air out through the caliper bleeders. It belongs after the reason for air entry has been repaired.
guides.why: A low or spongy pedal can come from a leak or trapped air, but it can also have other causes. Bleeding cannot repair a leaking connection, a faulty master cylinder or a damaged hose. The brake diagnostic chart separates these faults; starting there avoids treating a temporarily improved pedal as proof that the car is repaired.

when.summary: After a brake hydraulic component is disconnected, or when diagnosis identifies air after the leak or fault is repaired.
notes: Pressure bleeding is required after disconnecting a caliper, hose, tube or other brake hydraulic component. A newly installed master cylinder also needs the priming operation in Component Bleeding.
This is condition-based repair work. These procedures do not establish a calendar or mileage interval for flushing brake fluid.

prepare.title: Confirm the repair and brake configuration
prepare.detail: Identify the installed front caliper type, the rear parking-brake arrangement, and whether the car is left- or right-hand drive. Have the pressure-bleeding illustrations and the correct bleeder torque information available before opening a bleeder.

prepare.title: Use the specified fluid and clean equipment
prepare.detail: Use clean Motorcraft DOT 4 LV High Performance brake fluid, PM-20, meeting WSS-M6C65-A2. Prepare a brake/clutch pressure bleeder with a correctly fitting reservoir adapter, a clear bleed hose and a clean fluid container. Follow the equipment maker’s setup instructions.

prepare.title: Plan access and any ABS service operation
prepare.detail: Use the proper lifting and wheel-removal procedure. If a new hydraulic control unit has been installed, arrange a diagnostic scan tool capable of the ABS Service Bleed function before starting.

prepare.title: Protect nearby surfaces
prepare.detail: Clean around the reservoir cap before removal. If fluid spills, wash the affected component immediately with cold water; keep dirt and foreign material out of the fluid supply.

steps.title: Repair the cause and prime a new master cylinder
steps.body: Inspect for leaks and complete the hydraulic repair first. When the master cylinder is new, follow Component Bleeding to prime it with a master-cylinder bleeding set before bleeding the rest of the system. Do not use repeated bleeding to work around an unresolved leak.

steps.title: Set up a clean, pressurized fluid supply
steps.body: Fill the reservoir with the specified fluid and attach the correct pressure-bleeder adapter. Make sure the tank holds enough clean fluid for the operation, then connect it as its manufacturer directs. The pressure-bleeding procedure specifies 207–345 kPa (30–50 psi).

steps.title: Use the wheel sequence for the car’s steering layout
steps.body: Remove the wheels as directed and use the left-hand-drive or right-hand-drive sequence illustration in Brake System Pressure Bleeding. The two sequences differ. Keep that diagram open rather than substituting a remembered “furthest wheel first” order.

steps.title: Clear each caliper, including its additional bleeders
steps.body: Remove a bleeder cap if fitted. Partly fill a clean container with specified fluid, connect the hose and keep its outlet submerged. Open the bleeder 180 degrees and allow fluid to flow until it is clear and bubble-free, then close it to the confirmed specification. Four- and six-piston front calipers require the inner bleeder before the outer one. At rear calipers with an integral parking brake, apply and release the parking brake five times, then reopen the bleeder 180 degrees until clear fluid flows; repeat as necessary. Complete the remaining wheel ends in the prescribed order.

steps.title: Complete the extra cycle when the hydraulic unit is new
steps.body: For a newly installed ABS hydraulic control unit, perform the diagnostic tool’s ABS Service Bleed operation and then repeat the complete pressure-bleeding procedure. The first pressure bleed alone does not finish this repair.

steps.title: Release pressure, restore the level and verify operation
steps.body: Reinstall bleeder caps where fitted, lower the vehicle as directed, close the pressure-tank valve and release its pressure before removing the equipment. Fill the reservoir to the correct level and install its cap. Refit the wheels using their full installation instructions, inspect for leaks and confirm normal brake operation before the controlled road test required by the procedure.

watchFor.title: The pedal still sinks or feels spongy
watchFor.body: Return to the brake diagnostic chart. It distinguishes leaks and air from master-cylinder, hose, caliper and hydraulic-control-unit faults; an unresolved pedal concern is not a completed bleed.

watchFor.title: A six-piston torque discrepancy
watchFor.body: The available six-piston front-bleeder torque entry contains an inconsistent unit pair. Confirm the correct specification for the fitted caliper before tightening; do not choose one of the conflicting values by assumption.

watchFor.title: Air introduced during setup
watchFor.body: An unprimed replacement master cylinder, a dirty connection or an inadequate fluid supply can undermine the work. Finish the required preparation before moving through the wheel sequence.

notes: The rear parking-brake cycling instruction applies to calipers with the integral parking-brake arrangement described in the procedure.

procedures.purpose: Complete pressure-bleeding sequence, illustrated wheel order and new-HCU finishing steps.
Prime a new master cylinder and identify when disconnected hydraulic components require pressure bleeding.
Diagnose low, spongy or sinking brake-pedal symptoms before choosing bleeding as the repair.
Check the required fluid and fitted-brake specifications; note the six-piston torque discrepancy explained above.
Remove and reinstall wheels with the correct seating, tightening and recheck instructions.

guides.title: Cooling-system pressure testing: follow the leak evidence
guides.summary: Use a cold inspection, a separate cap check and a controlled pressure test to narrow down coolant loss before choosing a repair.

applicability.equipment: Factory cooling system; select the engine-specific diagnostic article.

guides.introduction: The cooling system holds coolant while allowing its pressure and volume to change as the engine warms and cools. Hoses, seals, joints and the expansion bottle must contain that fluid. A pressure tester gives the system a controlled load with the engine stopped, making a leak easier to investigate. The cap is tested separately because a poor cap seal and a leak elsewhere need different attention. On these engines the pressure cap is on the expansion, or degas, bottle; there is no radiator cap to remove.
guides.why: Finding the escaping fluid or the failed pressure check gives a repair a useful starting point. Coolant loss, overheating and slow warm-up have separate diagnostic paths. A successful pressure test alone does not establish that a fan, thermostat or coolant pump is working correctly.

when.summary: When coolant loss or an engine-specific diagnostic path calls for a cooling-system pressure test.
notes: This is a diagnostic check, with no mileage-based pressure-testing interval in these procedures.
Start with the relevant 2.3L, 3.7L or 5.0L article below. Their pressure-test values agree, but their component layouts and diagnostic branches must stay with the fitted engine.

prepare.title: Let the system become cold
prepare.detail: > **WARNING:** Stop the engine and allow it to cool before opening the cooling system. A hot or running engine can release pressurized steam and coolant when the cap is loosened, causing serious injury.

prepare.title: Have both tester adapters
prepare.detail: The cap and the bottle use different adapter arrangements. The procedures list a cap adapter equivalent to Snap-On TA53 and a bottle adapter equivalent to TA52, AST ASSFZ-47 or Redline RDL95-0750. Use a suitable pressure tester and the full equipment instructions.

prepare.title: Keep the observations together
prepare.detail: Record the cold level, the circumstances of any loss, visible wetness or residue, coolant odor, and retrieved cooling-related fault codes. Correct an obvious identified fault before extending the diagnosis.

steps.title: Begin with the cold visual check
steps.body: With the engine off and cold, inspect the level in the degas bottle and adjust it with the specified coolant as needed. Look for leaks or damage at hoses, tubes, clamps, housings, the radiator, bottle and coolant pump. A wet cabin floor or coolant odor inside also belongs in the inspection record because the heater core is part of the circuit.

steps.title: Inspect the sealing surfaces and test the cap separately
steps.body: Inspect the cap and bottle neck for damaged seals, cross-threading, burrs or other sealing defects. Use the cap adapter to test the cap. Its specified holding pressure is **145 kPa ± 21 kPa (21 psi ± 3 psi)**. Follow the engine-specific directions for a defective cap or bottle; the cap test value is a separate specification from the system test below.

steps.title: Pressurize the system slowly
steps.body:
Attach the correct bottle adapter. Increase pressure gradually to **124–138 kPa (18–20 psi)**; pressing the pump too quickly can produce a misleading reading.

> **NOTICE:** Do not exceed the cooling-system maximum in the engine-specific specifications. The cap rating is not permission to apply a higher system-test pressure.

steps.title: Observe the gauge and look for an external leak
steps.body: Watch the gauge for approximately **two minutes**. The procedure expects no pressure drop during that period. If pressure falls, inspect for escaping coolant and repair the identified leak. Record what actually became wet rather than replacing the nearest major component by assumption.

steps.title: Follow the internal-leak branch when needed
steps.body: If pressure drops without a visible external leak, inspect the coolant for engine oil and the engine oil for coolant. The loss-of-coolant diagnostic path also checks for combustion gases using the specified type of leak tester and its instructions. Contamination or a positive combustion-gas result leads into engine diagnosis; a pressure loss by itself does not identify a particular gasket.

steps.title: Close the test and verify the repair
steps.body: Use the tester instructions to release pressure safely before removing its adapter. Refit the bottle cap to its hard stop. After a cause is corrected, follow the engine-specific procedure to confirm normal operation and any required refill or bleeding work. Keep the initial and final results with the repair record.

watchFor.title: Falling pressure with no visible wet area
watchFor.body: Continue through the internal-leak checks instead of treating the absence of a puddle as proof that the system is sealed.

watchFor.title: Oil and coolant appearing to mix
watchFor.body: Oil in the coolant, coolant in the engine oil, or a positive combustion-gas test calls for the relevant engine diagnosis.

watchFor.title: A coolant color change without contamination
watchFor.body: The specified orange coolant can become pink or light red in normal use. Clear, uncontaminated fluid with that change alone is not a reason to flush the system.

notes: Keep cap testing, system pressure testing and combustion-gas testing as separate checks. Each answers a different diagnostic question.
Pressure testing does not replace the engine-specific coolant filling and bleeding procedure when the system has been opened for repair.

procedures.purpose: Use the 2.3L loss-of-coolant path and Cooling System Pressure Test.
Use the 3.7L loss-of-coolant path and Cooling System Pressure Test.
Use the 5.0L loss-of-coolant path and Cooling System Pressure Test.
Review the cooling-system pressure and hot-coolant precautions before opening it.

guides.title: Battery testing, charging and replacement: follow the evidence
guides.summary: Separate a low charge from a failed battery, choose the right next step, and plan the reset required for a replacement.
guides.introduction: A flat battery describes what happened, not why it happened. The battery may be discharged after storage, unable to hold up under load, or connected through a poor terminal or ground. Testing separates those possibilities. The job is finished when the battery, its connections and any underlying drain have been addressed—not merely when the engine starts once.
guides.why: A partly charged battery can give a misleading test result. Charging it properly before the required retest helps avoid replacing a serviceable battery. Equally, fitting a new battery without investigating an excessive key-off drain can leave the next one with the same problem.

when.summary: When starting becomes weak, a battery is discharged, or a test result calls for charging or replacement.
notes: Use the battery’s condition and diagnostic result; there is no fixed replacement interval in this guide.
Extended storage and repeated short moves with heavy electrical loads can discharge a battery. Fifteen minutes of idling is not an adequate recovery plan for a deeply discharged battery.

prepare.title: Use suitable diagnostic equipment
prepare.detail: Arrange an approved diagnostic battery charger/tester and follow its instructions. For a new battery, plan access to a scan tool that can perform the Battery Monitoring System reset.

prepare.title: Protect yourself and the work area
prepare.detail: Wear eye protection, provide ventilation, and keep sparks and flames away from the battery. Read the linked battery precautions before handling its acid-containing case or terminals.

prepare.title: Plan disconnection and reconnection
prepare.detail: The disconnect article distinguishes interrupting vehicle power at the negative cable from removing both cables for battery testing or replacement. Use the sequence required by the actual operation.

steps.title: Inspect the connections before condemning the battery
steps.body: With the ignition off, inspect the battery, its mounting, terminals, wiring and chassis grounds. Correct dirty or loose connections and retest; a poor electrical path can resemble a battery failure.

steps.title: Test the battery with the correct equipment
steps.body: Follow the battery-condition test and the charger/analyzer’s decision. The test evaluates how the battery behaves under the specified load; a voltage reading without the required test conditions does not give the same answer.

steps.title: Charge a discharged battery properly
steps.body: Follow Battery Charging: disconnect the battery, connect the charger to the battery posts with correct polarity, and follow the charger instructions. A cold battery needs to reach approximately 5°C (41°F) before charging; the procedure notes that warming at room temperature may take four to eight hours.

steps.title: Retest and follow the result
steps.body: Complete charging before the required retest. A REPLACE BATTERY or REPLACE-BAD CELL result calls for replacement through the linked procedure. If the battery passes but repeatedly goes flat, continue with drain diagnosis instead of assuming another battery will fix it.

steps.title: Install only when replacement is justified
steps.body: Use the exact battery removal/installation and cable procedures. They cover the hold-down, connection sequence and tightening requirements. Support the battery with a carrier or at opposite corners rather than squeezing its end walls.

steps.title: Complete the reset and check the original concern
steps.body: After a new battery is connected, use the scan tool to perform the Battery Monitoring System (BMS) reset. A recharge alone is not the new-battery replacement step. Disconnection can temporarily affect adaptive driving behavior; follow applicable relearn or window-initialization instructions and verify the original starting concern.

watchFor.title: It goes flat again after a full charge
watchFor.body: Move to the parasitic-drain guide and confirm the cause before spending money on another battery.

watchFor.title: The test changes after charging or terminal repair
watchFor.body: Keep the sequence and results in the service record. The initial low-charge result is not interchangeable with the final condition result.

watchFor.title: A damaged or leaking case
watchFor.body: Stop handling it as a routine charging job and follow the battery safety precautions.

notes: Battery Monitoring System reset requires the specified scan-tool function. Clearing a warning message is not the same operation.
The linked procedures contain the complete safety precautions and fastener requirements; this guide helps choose and plan the correct work.

procedures.purpose: Perform the battery-condition test and follow its charging, replacement or drain-test branches.
Charge a discharged battery with the correct preparation and charger procedure.
Disconnect and reconnect the battery cables in the correct sequence.
Replace a confirmed faulty battery and complete the BMS reset.
Review battery handling, acid and explosive-gas precautions.
Initialize one-touch windows when the applicable procedure calls for it.

guides.title: Wheel alignment: turn tire wear into a useful measurement
guides.summary: Understand toe and camber, check what can upset the readings, and plan an alignment that fixes the cause of uneven wear.

applicability.equipment: Factory suspension geometry; modified suspension needs its own applicable specifications.

guides.introduction: Alignment describes where the wheels point and how they lean. Toe is the direction a wheel points when viewed from above; camber is its inward or outward lean when viewed from the front or rear. A small error can make a tire scrub across the road instead of rolling cleanly. Getting the angles right starts with healthy tires and suspension, not immediately turning an adjustment bolt.
guides.why: An alignment check can help explain a crooked steering wheel, uneven tire wear or a pull. Those symptoms can also come from tire pressure, tire forces, brake drag or loose suspension parts. Measuring after those basic checks prevents an adjustment from hiding another problem.

when.summary: Check when tire wear, pulling or an off-center steering wheel points to an alignment concern.
notes: This is a condition-based check, with no fixed alignment mileage added here.
Use the final alignment checks required by the relevant suspension or steering repair. Lowered or otherwise modified cars need specifications appropriate to that configuration.

prepare.title: Collect the clues
prepare.detail: Note where the tires are wearing, when the car pulls, and whether steering or suspension work has recently been done. Keep any previous alignment readings.

prepare.title: Start with a sound car
prepare.detail: Use the correct cold tire pressures and tire sizes. Check for damage, uneven loading and worn or loose steering and suspension components before measuring.

prepare.title: Arrange an alignment system
prepare.detail: This job uses a level alignment platform and calibrated equipment. An alignment shop can supply measured before-and-after values and carry out any necessary adjustments.

steps.title: Separate the symptom from the diagnosis
steps.body: A car that pulls is giving you a clue, not an automatic alignment verdict. Use the suspension diagnosis article to work through loading, tires, brake drag and steering condition before deciding which angle is wrong.

steps.title: Measure all relevant angles before adjusting
steps.body: With the car set up according to the equipment instructions, record front and rear readings against the specification for its fitted suspension. Keep the steering wheel centered. Looking at all four wheels helps avoid correcting the front while overlooking the rear.

steps.title: Make only the adjustment the readings support
steps.body: Front toe is adjusted at the tie rods; rear toe uses the toe-link adjustment. The steering bellows must not twist as the front tie rods turn. The rear adjustment area must be clean so the hardware clamps correctly. Use the linked procedure for the actual movement and tightening steps.

steps.title: Treat camber correction as its own job
steps.body: Changing camber can also alter toe, so toe needs another check afterward. Rear camber has a control-arm adjustment. The linked front-camber correction involves special service fasteners and modification at the strut mounting hole; it is an advanced repair decision for a suitably equipped shop, not a bolt to loosen experimentally.

steps.title: Verify after final tightening
steps.body: Recheck the readings after the fasteners are tightened to their procedure-specific values. The wheels can move as the joints clamp. Save the final readings, then confirm straight-ahead steering and the original complaint on a controlled road test.

steps.title: Follow up on the tire wear
steps.body: Record the present wear pattern so the next inspection can show whether it is progressing. Existing damage will not disappear after adjustment. If the car still pulls with correct readings, continue the tire, brake and steering diagnosis instead of pushing the alignment outside specification.

watchFor.title: Alignment will not hold
watchFor.body: Loose joints, damaged components or a clamping problem need correction before another adjustment is likely to last.

watchFor.title: An angle outside the available adjustment
watchFor.body: Check ride height and component condition. Do not substitute arbitrary settings or modify suspension parts simply to make a display turn green.

watchFor.title: A changed suspension setup
watchFor.body: Factory alignment specifications are not automatically suitable for aftermarket suspension and wheel changes.

notes: This guide explains the inspection and planning sequence. The linked adjustment articles carry the fastener requirements and exact work steps.
Do not confuse wheel balancing with alignment: balancing addresses rotating mass; alignment addresses wheel direction and lean.

procedures.purpose: Work through pulling, tire wear, ride height and suspension condition before an adjustment.
Adjust front toe and protect the steering bellows while turning the tie rods.
Adjust rear toe, keep the clamping surfaces clean and verify the final readings.
Correct rear camber and recheck rear toe afterward.
Review the specialist front-camber correction and its required service fasteners.

guides.title: Bleed the MT82 clutch hydraulic circuit

applicability.equipment: MT82 six-speed manual transmission only; not the automatic transmission or the 5.2L/TR-3160 clutch system.

guides.summary: Restore a consistent clutch pedal after hydraulic repair or a confirmed air problem using the MT82 reservoir-vacuum procedure.
guides.introduction: The clutch pedal operates a master cylinder, which moves fluid through a tube to the slave cylinder at the transmission. That movement releases the clutch so the transmission can shift. Trapped air can absorb part of the pedal stroke, leaving less movement available to release the clutch even when the pedal is pressed.
guides.why: A soft pedal, clutch drag or difficult shifting can involve air, low fluid or a leak, but the same symptoms can also involve the master cylinder, slave cylinder or clutch parts. The MT82 diagnostic chart checks these possibilities. Bleeding is useful when air is the problem; it does not fix worn friction parts or a leaking cylinder.

when.summary: After MT82 clutch hydraulic repair, or when diagnosis identifies trapped air causing poor release or a soft pedal.
notes: The clutch-master-cylinder installation procedure explicitly calls for hydraulic bleeding. The MT82 diagnostic chart also calls for it when air is involved in clutch drag, difficult shifting or an unusually soft pedal.
There is no fixed clutch-fluid flush interval established by these repair instructions. This guide does not apply to the 5.2L/TR-3160 system.

prepare.title: Verify the transmission and fluid circuit
prepare.detail: Confirm that the car has the MT82 transmission. Inspect fluid level and hydraulic connections, and repair leaks before bleeding. The brake and clutch circuits share the reservoir, so a low level also calls for inspection of the brake system.

prepare.title: Have the specified fluid ready
prepare.detail: Use Motorcraft DOT 4 LV High Performance brake fluid, PM-20, meeting WSS-M6C65-A2. The reservoir must be filled to MAX during the procedure. Read the fluid product’s handling precautions and protect painted and plastic surfaces.

prepare.title: Prepare a sealed vacuum connection
prepare.detail: Use the specified vacuum pump kit with an airtight reservoir stopper. The procedure permits a 50 mm (1.96 in) rubber stopper with an 8 mm (0.31 in) pipe as the alternative connection. This is a reservoir-vacuum operation, not an instruction to apply brake-bleeder pressure.

prepare.title: Keep the correct references open
prepare.detail: Use Clutch System Bleeding for the complete illustrated sequence and Manual Transmission diagnosis for the clutch-pedal reserve check after bleeding.

steps.title: Check the connections and start with the pedal fully up
steps.body: Make sure all hydraulic tubes are correctly seated, the repaired circuit is leak-free and the clutch pedal is in its fully raised position. Fill the brake/clutch reservoir to MAX with the specified fluid.

steps.title: Apply and release the reservoir vacuum
steps.body: Fit the airtight stopper and connect the vacuum pump. Hold the stopper in place, draw 15–20 inches of vacuum and hold it for one minute. Release the vacuum quickly, then remove the stopper and equipment.

steps.title: Restore the fluid level and work the pedal
steps.body: Refill the reservoir to MAX and fit the cap. Press and release the clutch pedal 10–12 times, or until the effort is consistent and positive at the top of travel. This checks whether the initial portion of the pedal stroke now produces a dependable hydraulic response.

steps.title: Repeat the specified vacuum and pedal cycle
steps.body: Repeat the vacuum-hold/release, refill/cap and pedal-cycling sequence two additional times, or until there is consistent, positive pedal effort at the top, as directed in the bleeding procedure. Do not continue indefinitely if the fluid level drops or the result remains inconsistent; investigate the fault.

steps.title: Confirm reserve and normal clutch operation
steps.body: Install the reservoir cap and check clutch-pedal reserve using the complete MT82 diagnostic method. That method uses 1 in (25 mm) as the minimum acceptable reserve; it is not a pedal-adjustment instruction. Check normal clutch operation and return to the symptom chart if release or shifting remains poor.

watchFor.title: The fluid level falls again
watchFor.body: Inspect the clutch and brake hydraulic systems for leaks. Topping up or bleeding repeatedly does not resolve fluid loss.

watchFor.title: A soft pedal remains after the prescribed cycles
watchFor.body: Check the master cylinder for external leakage and the slave cylinder for leakage or binding, following the MT82 symptom chart.

watchFor.title: A hard pedal or clutch slip
watchFor.body: These symptoms have separate diagnostic paths. Binding parts, worn friction components and a clutch that will not retract are not automatically an air problem.

watchFor.title: Spilled fluid
watchFor.body: Immediately wash fluid off painted or plastic surfaces with water to avoid damage.

notes: The guide’s engine filter identifies the 2015 2.3L, 3.7L and 5.0L range; the MT82 equipment requirement still has to match the actual car.
The clutch-pedal reserve test involves vehicle operation. Follow its complete setup and method rather than interpreting the reserve number as a static ruler measurement.

procedures.purpose: Complete MT82 reservoir-vacuum bleeding sequence, equipment and fluid requirements.
Diagnose clutch symptoms and perform the clutch-pedal reserve test.
Locate the clutch pedal, master cylinder, slave cylinder and hydraulic tubes.
Left-hand-drive master-cylinder replacement, including its required bleeding step.

guides.title: Diagnose brake pulsation and disc runout
guides.summary: Separate normal ABS feedback from brake roughness, inspect disc and hub seating, and use the correct runout and thickness limits before choosing a repair.
guides.introduction: Runout is the side-to-side movement of an installed brake disc as it rotates. A disc, its mating surfaces and the way the wheel is tightened all contribute to the assembled result. Pulsation is a symptom rather than proof that a disc needs replacing: normal ABS operation, brake condition and suspension faults must be distinguished first.
guides.why: Replacing or machining a disc without checking how it seats can leave the underlying problem in place. The wheel-installation instructions specifically warn that incorrect tightening order can produce high disc runout and accelerate brake roughness. Measuring the installed assembly and checking its mounting surfaces makes the repair decision more useful than judging the disc by appearance alone.

when.summary: When braking repeatedly causes speed-related pedal pulsation, steering-wheel nibble or shudder outside normal ABS operation.
notes: The brake diagnostic chart distinguishes pulsation with ABS activity on loose, wet or snowy surfaces from a repeatable brake or suspension concern.
This is a condition-based diagnostic task, not a scheduled rotor-machining service. Noise alone is not a reason to machine a disc.

prepare.title: Record the symptom before disassembly
prepare.detail: Note whether vibration appears under braking or continues with the pedal released, and whether it is felt in the pedal, steering wheel or seat. Use the brake diagnostic chart to select the correct path and safe test conditions.

prepare.title: Identify the fitted brake package
prepare.detail: Select the actual front caliper and rear disc type before using thickness limits or removing parts. The specification table has different minimum disc thicknesses for the two-, four- and six-piston front systems and for solid versus vented rear discs.

prepare.title: Prepare measuring and support equipment
prepare.detail: Arrange a reliable installed-disc runout measurement with appropriate dial-indicator equipment and a disc-thickness measurement. Have proper lifting equipment, a torque wrench and a way to support a removed caliper without loading its hose.

prepare.title: Plan the measurement boundary
prepare.detail: The linked specifications give an installed-disc runout limit. They do not provide a separate hub-flange runout setup or tolerance, so do not condemn a hub by applying the disc limit to the bare hub.

steps.title: Confirm that the symptom needs brake diagnosis
steps.body: Follow the Brake System vibration pinpoint test. Normal ABS operation can cause hydraulic-unit noise and pedal pulsation during heavy braking or on low-grip surfaces. A repeatable speed-related nibble or shudder can involve brake or suspension components and needs the corresponding inspection.

steps.title: Inspect the mountings before blaming the disc
steps.body: Check the relevant suspension components and wheel installation. If a disc is removed, clean its mating surfaces with the specified brake-cleaning material and a wire brush as directed. Keep the caliper supported; never let it hang by its hose. Corrosion, dirt and incorrect seating must be addressed before relying on an assembled measurement.

steps.title: Record installed-disc runout against its own limit
steps.body: Have the installed disc measured with a repeatable, correctly secured gauge setup and record the indicated lateral movement. The listed maximum installed brake-disc runout is 0.05 mm (0.002 in). Treat that as an assembled-disc criterion, not a separate hub-flange tolerance. If the result is excessive, investigate seating and component condition rather than automatically replacing the hub.

steps.title: Check thickness and whether machining is permitted
steps.body: Measure disc thickness and compare it with the exact fitted-brake specification. Machining is not allowed for discs with cross-drilled friction surfaces. A disc must not be machined when its thickness is less than the minimum thickness plus 0.6 mm (0.0236 in). This machining allowance is separate from the final minimum-thickness limit.

steps.title: Choose a repair that addresses the measured condition
steps.body: Use the brake diagnosis and disc condition to decide whether cleaning and correct installation, disc replacement or permitted machining is appropriate. Where machining is selected, the procedure requires an on-vehicle lathe rather than a bench lathe; follow its complete setup, runout adjustment and post-cut thickness checks. Do not machine simply to treat squeal or other brake noise.

steps.title: Reassemble correctly and verify the original complaint
steps.body: Use the correct front or rear disc procedure, including fasteners that must be replaced. Clean the wheel and hub mating surfaces and tighten wheel nuts in the prescribed star pattern with clean, dry threads. Apply the brake pedal several times after disc work to verify operation, then complete the appropriate controlled road test. Recheck wheel-nut tightness within 100 mi (160 km) after wheel installation.

watchFor.title: Runout and thickness are different measurements
watchFor.body: A disc can meet one requirement and fail another. Keep the installed runout result, measured thickness and correct package-specific minimum together in the job record.

watchFor.title: Loose or damaged suspension parts
watchFor.body: The brake vibration pinpoint test checks suspension condition as well as discs. Correct the identified fault instead of repeatedly machining rotors.

watchFor.title: The wrong brake-package limit is used
watchFor.body: Match the front caliper and rear disc configuration before using thickness limits or choosing parts. Two-, four- and six-piston front brakes and solid versus vented rear discs do not all share the same minimum thickness.

watchFor.title: A hub is blamed without an applicable test
watchFor.body: No separate hub-flange runout limit is established by the linked material. Investigate seating and use an appropriate hub-specific diagnostic reference before condemning the hub.

notes: The 0.05 mm (0.002 in) value is the installed-disc limit; it must not be reused as a bare-hub tolerance. The machining article separately specifies the lathe’s adjustment conditions.
Use a suitably equipped brake shop for a reliable installed-disc measurement, and follow the complete linked procedure when carrying out the repair.

guides.title: Measure wheel vibration and match the tire to the rim
guides.summary: Use loaded road-force or radial-runout measurements to identify the high spot, reposition a tire when appropriate and finish with correct wheel-to-hub seating.
guides.introduction: A wheel-and-tire assembly can be balanced yet still feel rough because it is not perfectly round or does not deflect evenly under load. Balancing corrects uneven mass; runout and road-force testing investigate a different source of vibration. Match mounting changes the tire’s position on the rim so their combined variation can be reduced before parts are replaced.
guides.why: A loaded road-force test measures how the tire behaves against a roller, while an unloaded dial indicator measures its shape. The diagnostic procedure prefers loaded testing for judging tire serviceability. Careful marking and repeat measurements help distinguish a tire contribution from a wheel contribution, and proper hub seating prevents the final installation from introducing another offset.

when.summary: When diagnosis points to a wheel/tire vibration that persists after basic tire, pressure and wheel-condition checks.
notes: Do not perform this tire/wheel vibration diagnosis on tires with fewer than 200 mi (322 km) in service; initial flat spotting can change during that period. This does not postpone correcting obvious damage or unsafe tire condition.
Before runout matching, remove temporary flat spotting by driving 20 or more miles immediately before measurement, as directed in the matching procedure.
This is diagnostic correction when a concern is present, not a mileage-based tire-matching service.

prepare.title: Start with sound, correctly inflated tires
prepare.detail: Inspect for damage, bent wheels and loose fasteners, and use the recommended tire size and wheel specification. Set the specified pressure from the vehicle’s tire label using an accurate digital gauge. Keep each assembly’s vehicle position marked.

prepare.title: Use equipment that centers and protects the wheel
prepare.detail: Use the correct balancer adapters and clean assemblies. Incorrect centering can create an apparent runout problem. The wheel procedure requires suitable center-clamp tire-changing equipment and balancing equipment that does not contact the wheel face.

prepare.title: Choose the approved measurement and matching method
prepare.detail: Loaded Hunter Road Force measurement is preferred. A securely mounted dial indicator can measure radial runout at the center tread rib, but an unloaded reading alone cannot decide whether a tire should be removed from service.

prepare.title: Have TPMS-safe tire service and marking materials ready
prepare.detail: Prepare tire chalk or crayon, the tire-changing procedure, fast-drying, corrosion-inhibiting bead lubricant and wheel-installation instructions. Tire rotation on the rim must protect the pressure sensor and reseat the beads correctly.

steps.title: Measure and mark the baseline
steps.body: After the condition checks and flat-spot warm-up, mark the assembly’s vehicle position and measure using the correct adapters. Loaded road force above 20 lb (9 kg) calls for match mounting; a value at or below that limit leads to balancing and wheel-to-hub optimization. With the dial-indicator method, measure the center tread rib from its zeroed low spot through a complete revolution; assembly runout above 1.14 mm (0.045 in) calls for matching. Record the high spot and reading.

steps.title: Select the right matching path for the machine
steps.body: Use only the Ford-approved Hunter method described in Wheel to Tire Runout Minimization, or its manual matching sequence. Generation I/II machines supply readings only. Generation III uses “Match Without Rim Runout” when available; otherwise use the manual sequence. Generation IV/V uses “180 Matching.” Do not assume another automatic matching prompt is equivalent.

steps.title: Reposition the tire and take the second measurement
steps.body: For the manual method, place a reference mark on the tire at the valve stem, break the beads using the TPMS precautions, lubricate them as directed and rotate the tire 180 degrees on the wheel. The reference mark is now opposite the valve stem. Reinflate correctly and remeasure, marking the new high spot and reading. If the result is within the applicable limit, proceed to balancing and hub optimization.

steps.title: Use the high spots to choose the next branch
steps.body: If two above-limit measurements keep the high spots within 4 in (101.6 mm) of each other on the tire, the tire is the likely contributor; the procedure requires both measurements before that conclusion. If the second high spot is within 4 in (101.6 mm) of the opposite position of the first high spot on the wheel, inspect the bare wheel and measure its runout; the matching procedure specifies replacement above 1.14 mm (0.0449 in). If neither pattern fits and the result remains high, follow the illustrated 90-degree tire repositioning branch. Do not replace a tire merely because one unloaded reading was high.

steps.title: Balance the corrected assembly and optimize hub seating
steps.body: Permanently mark the final high spot and reading on the inner sidewall and balance the assembly. For wheel-to-hub optimization, place its high spot at 6 o’clock and hand-snug the nuts. Lower the tire until it just contacts the ground and slightly loads the suspension, then tighten as directed. During this specific optimization operation, do not let the full vehicle weight rest on the tire while tightening.

steps.title: Finish the installation and confirm the result
steps.body: Use the wheel procedure for clean mating surfaces, the specified torque and star pattern. Keep lubricant away from wheel-stud and wheel-nut threads and from brake friction surfaces. Verify whether the original vibration has improved and continue the diagnostic path if it has not. Recheck wheel-nut tightness within 100 mi (160 km) after installation.

watchFor.title: A false reading caused by setup
watchFor.body: Dirt, the wrong balancer adapter or movement of the dial-indicator stand can imitate an assembly fault. Confirm repeatable setup before making a parts decision.

watchFor.title: A tire condemned from unloaded runout alone
watchFor.body: The diagnostic instructions say unloaded runout cannot accurately determine tire serviceability. Loaded testing and the complete diagnostic branch matter.

watchFor.title: A wheel-to-hub exception is missed
watchFor.body: The runout-optimization procedure deliberately uses only slight tire loading while tightening. Keep that special instruction with this operation rather than blindly applying the general installation wording about the vehicle resting on its tires.

watchFor.title: Damage during tire service
watchFor.body: Use the TPMS precautions, approved wheel-clamping approach and appropriate lubricant. Correcting vibration is not a reason to risk a pressure sensor or wheel finish.

notes: Road-force and geometric runout use different units and answer different questions; 20 lb is a force threshold, not a tire-pressure setting.

The matching article rounds the bare-wheel limit to 0.0449 in while the diagnostic article gives 0.045 in for the assembly criterion; both metric values are 1.14 mm. Keep the wheel and assembly decisions in their respective branches.

guides.title: Parasitic battery drain: find what stays awake
guides.summary: Measure current after the car has settled, then isolate the circuit that is drawing too much instead of guessing at a module.
guides.introduction: Some electrical use continues after the ignition is switched off. The diagnostic question is whether the car settles to the expected resting draw, or whether a lamp, circuit or module keeps consuming too much. The tricky part is preserving the car’s state while measuring it: opening a circuit or waking a module can change the very behavior you are trying to observe.
guides.why: A current reading taken too soon can mistake normal module activity for a fault. A power interruption can also reset a troublesome module and temporarily hide the drain. A deliberate setup makes the final number meaningful.

when.summary: When a charged, tested battery repeatedly loses charge while the vehicle is parked.
notes: This is condition-based diagnosis, not a periodic maintenance service.
Do not begin with a discharged battery or an active low-battery message. Charge and test the battery first.

prepare.title: Prepare the correct measuring equipment
prepare.detail: The procedure specifies an inline ammeter capable of reading milliamps with a 10-amp capability, plus a 30-amp fused jumper used to preserve continuity during setup. A test lamp or voltage reading does not substitute for this current measurement.

prepare.title: Allow enough uninterrupted time
prepare.detail: Plan for at least 90 minutes of key-off settling, subject to equipment and regional differences, and for another settling period when the isolation procedure requires it.

prepare.title: Use the circuit information
prepare.detail: Have the fuse locations and relevant wiring information ready before beginning. A thermal camera can help identify activity, but the current measurement confirms the draw.

steps.title: Establish a sound starting point
steps.body: Fully charge and test the battery. Record the parking duration and conditions that lead to discharge. Follow the procedure’s activation drive—at least five minutes above 48 km/h (30 mph)—before setting up the resting test.

steps.title: Arrange access without keeping the car awake
steps.body: With ignition off, prepare hood, door-latch and fuse-box access exactly as the test describes so lamps do not remain on. Disable applicable approach or alarm features. On an automatic, verify that Park indication works; an incorrect indication can prevent modules from sleeping.

steps.title: Connect the meter without interrupting power
steps.body: Use the fused jumper and inline-meter connection sequence in Battery Drain Check. Lock the vehicle as directed and move all keys/fobs at least 50 feet away. If continuity is broken, or meter connections need changing, follow the jumper and power-down instructions rather than treating the earlier settling time as valid.

steps.title: Wait, then interpret the resting draw
steps.body: Keep the ignition off and allow at least 90 minutes for the modules to settle. Record the current. The procedure describes a 25–50 mA range depending on equipment and recommends comparison with a similar vehicle; one universal cutoff should not replace that context.

steps.title: Isolate the circuit, then the actual cause
steps.body: If draw is excessive, follow the staged fuse and component isolation sequence and note the current change. The first fuse that reduces the draw identifies a circuit, not automatically a failed component. Check whether a module is being kept awake by an input, and include aftermarket electrical connections when fitted.

steps.title: Finish the diagnosis and restore the vehicle
steps.body: If fused circuits do not explain the draw, follow the checks for other battery-fed circuits and the generator. Restore the test connections and equipment, carry out required window initialization, and verify that the excessive draw is gone after the prescribed settling period.

watchFor.title: The reading changes when you touch the setup
watchFor.body: A door event, key proximity or interrupted battery connection can change module activity. Restore the required test conditions before deciding a repair worked.

watchFor.title: A module appears to be the drain
watchFor.body: Investigate its inputs before replacing it. An input can keep an otherwise functioning module awake.

watchFor.title: Only a voltage reading is available
watchFor.body: Battery voltage alone does not locate a parasitic-current path; use the specified current test.

notes: This guide is an overview of an equipment-based electrical test. Keep the ignition off during the inline-current measurement. Never crank or start the engine, or switch on heavy electrical loads, with the inline ammeter connected. Follow the meter and fused-jumper sequence in the full procedure.
